2. Ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid (ocular cicatricial pemphigoid) — fits the pattern of progressive conjunctival cicatrization, subepithelial fibrosis, madarosis and punctal stenosis; biopsy can be false-negative, so remains a strong possibility.
3. Stevens–Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis sequelae with chronic cicatrizing conjunctivitis — can produce similar findings but usually follows a severe mucocutaneous reaction (less likely if no skin/mucous history).
4. Chronic blepharokeratoconjunctivitis (severe blepharitis/rosacea-associated) with secondary scarring — explains eyelid swelling and madarosis and can produce chronic conjunctival change, but less classically cicatrizing to the degree described.
5. Trachoma (chronic chlamydial conjunctivitis) — can cause conjunctival scarring, punctal stenosis and madarosis, but epidemiology and abrupt temporal relation to a new treatment make it less likely.
